A2.text:
Elif is from Istanbul. Last month, she visited her friend Nigar in Baku. On Saturday, Nigar took her to the Green Market.

The market was very crowded. There were hundreds of stalls with fresh fruit, vegetables, cheese and spices. A busker played the tar near the door.

Elif loved it. “In Istanbul, I always bargain at the market,” she said. “Let me try here.”

She stopped at a fruit stall. The vendor was an old man with a big smile. Elif asked about the pomegranates.

“Ten manats a kilo,” he said.

“That is a rip off!” Elif said in Turkish. “Five manats.”

The old man laughed. “Nine,” he said. He liked to drive a hard bargain. They talked for ten minutes. Elif could not win.

Then Nigar said, “My friend came from Istanbul to see Baku. She wants to try local pomegranates.”

The old man's face changed. “From Istanbul? My son lives there!” He put four big pomegranates in a bag. “This is a gift,” he said. “Today, my pomegranates go for a song.”

Elif was very happy. She thanked him many times.

Back in Istanbul, she told all her friends about the old man. Now, because of word of mouth, every Turkish tourist in Baku visits his stall.

B1.text:
When Elif came from Istanbul to spend a week with her university friend Nigar, the first place she wanted to see in Baku wasn't the Flame Towers or the Old City. It was a market. “You learn more about a city from its markets than from its museums,” she said.

So on Saturday morning, Nigar took her to the Green Market. It was crowded with shoppers carrying bags of herbs. There were stalls piled high with tomatoes, mountains of white cheese and sacks of saffron.

Elif was delighted. “In Istanbul, nobody pays the first price,” she said, rolling up her sleeves. “Watch and learn.”

She chose a fruit stall run by an elderly vendor with a grey moustache and a pile of enormous red pomegranates.

“How much?” she asked in Turkish.

“Ten manats a kilo.”

Elif gasped dramatically. “Ten? That's a complete rip off! I'll give you five.”

The vendor smiled the smile of a man who had been selling fruit for forty years. “Nine.” He clearly enjoyed driving a hard bargain. For ten minutes they went back and forth — eight and a half, six, eight, six and a half — and the old man wouldn't move another coin.

Finally, Nigar stepped in. “My friend came all the way from Istanbul,” she explained in Azerbaijani. “She wanted to taste local pomegranates.”

The vendor's eyebrows went up. “Istanbul? My son has lived in Kadıköy for twelve years!” He started filling a bag with the best fruit on the stall. “Put your money away. For guests from Istanbul, pomegranates go for a song today — in fact, they go for nothing.”

Elif tried to pay three times. He refused three times.

When she returned home, she told the story to everyone she knew, wrote down the exact location of his stall. Word of mouth did the rest. These days, the old man says, at least two Turkish tourists a week arrive at his stall asking for “the pomegranates from the story”.

B2.text:
When Elif flew in from Istanbul to spend a week with her old university friend Nigar, she skipped the Flame Towers entirely on her first morning. “Museums tell you what a city wants you to think,” she announced. “Markets tell you what it actually is.”

So Nigar took her to the Green Market, which on a Saturday morning was crowded to the point of choreography — shoppers weaving between handcarts, arms full of coriander and tarragon, the air thick with the scent of warm bread and dried apricots. Stalls groaned under pyramids of tomatoes, wheels of white cheese and burlap sacks of saffron. By the entrance, a busker coaxed a melancholy tune from his tar while a small boy danced with great seriousness in front of him.

Elif was in her element. “In Istanbul,” she said, cracking her knuckles, “only tourists pay the first price. Prepare to be impressed.”

She selected a fruit stall presided over by an elderly vendor with a magnificent grey moustache and a heap of pomegranates the size of grapefruits.

“How much?” she asked in Turkish.

“Ten manats a kilo.”

Elif clutched her heart. “Ten? That's daylight robbery — a total rip off! Five.”

The old man smiled with the serenity of four decades behind a counter. “Nine.” It was obvious that he enjoyed driving a hard bargain as much as she did. For ten minutes the figures flew back and forth — eight and a half, six, eight, six and a half — but he remained as immovable as the Maiden Tower.

Eventually Nigar intervened. “My friend has come all the way from Istanbul,” she told him in Azerbaijani. “Above all, she wanted to taste local pomegranates.”

The vendor's eyebrows shot up. “Istanbul? My son has lived in Kadıköy for twelve years!” He began filling a bag with the finest fruit on the stall. “Put that purse away. For guests from Istanbul, pomegranates go for a song today — or rather, for no song at all.”

Elif attempted to pay three times; three times she was refused with growing indignation.

Back home, she told the story to anyone who would listen, posted a photo of the vendor beside his pyramid and shared the precise location of his stall. Word of mouth handled the rest. According to the old man, scarcely a week now passes without some Turkish visitor appearing at his counter and asking, a little shyly, for “the pomegranates from the story”.

podcast.title: A fifty-manat carpet

before.predict: Can you bargain at a market? Guess: what did Sam pay too much for in the Old City?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is street life and markets. And this morning I was at the Green Market — Yashil Bazar.
On a Saturday? It's so crowded!
Very. But I love it. The colours, the smells, the people shouting prices.
What did you buy?
Tomatoes, cheese, herbs — everything so fresh. And pomegranates from one stall where the man gave me three for free.
Because you smiled at him. [laugh] Did you try to bargain?
No… I just paid what he asked.
You should go with my grandmother. She can drive a hard bargain like nobody else.
What does she do?
She looks at the fruit, says it's not good, walks away — and the seller runs after her with a better price.
[laugh] Amazing. I need lessons. Last month in the Old City I paid fifty manat for a tiny carpet.
Fifty? For a small one? Sam, that's a rip off.
I know that now. The same carpet was twenty in a shop two streets away.
That is why you go where local people go.
How do you find those places?
Word of mouth. My neighbour Mr Aliyev told me about the best bread stall — a tandir oven right on the street.
Bread from a tandir — I could live on that. But what I really love on Nizami Street are the buskers.
The violin player near the fountain? He's been there for years.
I always stop and give him a few coins. He makes the whole street feel alive.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: where do you like to shop — at a market, in a shop or online? And can you bargain?
Send me your tips. I need them. See you next time!
Bye for now!
